promptText: What is the key difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: git fetch only downloads remote commits into remote-tracking branches without touching your working branch, while git pull additionally merges or rebases them into it
git fetch and git pull are exactly identical commands with different names
git fetch merges remote changes into your branch, while git pull only downloads without merging
git pull only works with GitHub, while git fetch works with any Git host
explanation: git fetch is safe and non-destructive - it updates remote-tracking refs like origin/main so you can inspect what changed before integrating; git pull is effectively fetch followed by an automatic merge (or rebase) into your current branch, which can trigger conflicts immediately.

promptText: What does a Git commit object actually store?
options: A pointer to a full snapshot tree of the tracked files, plus a pointer to its parent commit(s) and metadata - not a diff
Only the diff (the lines that changed) relative to the previous commit
A copy of every file in the repository as of that moment, duplicated in full even if unchanged
A list of file names that changed, without any content
explanation: A commit is an immutable snapshot of the entire tracked tree, storing a pointer to a tree object, author/committer metadata, and pointer(s) to parent commit(s) - Git computes diffs on demand for display, and deduplicates unchanged files via content-addressable storage, but the model is snapshots, not stored diffs.

promptText: A bad commit has already been pushed and pulled by teammates on a shared branch. What is the safe way to undo it?
options: git revert - it creates a new commit that undoes the change without rewriting existing history
git reset --hard - it destroys the commit and its changes cleanly
git reset --soft, since it keeps the changes staged for teammates to see
Deleting the branch and creating a new one with the same name
explanation: git reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer, which is only safe for local, unpushed work; git revert adds a new commit that undoes a previous one, making it safe for shared history since it never rewrites commits others already have.

promptText: Why is creating a new branch in Git essentially instantaneous, unlike branching in some older centralized systems?
options: A branch is just a small file containing a commit SHA - creating one only writes a new pointer, without copying any files
Git branches are created lazily and don't actually exist until the first commit is made on them
Branch creation is fast because Git compresses all files before branching
Git caches branches in memory so no disk write ever happens
explanation: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit - a small file under .git/refs/heads/ holding a SHA. Creating a branch just writes that pointer at the current commit with no file copying involved, which is why branching is cheap and instant.

promptText: What is git stash used for?
options: Shelving uncommitted changes temporarily so you can switch context (e.g. for an urgent hotfix), then restore them later
Permanently deleting uncommitted changes from the working directory
Creating a backup copy of the entire repository on the remote server
Combining several commits into a single commit before pushing
explanation: git stash push shelves your in-progress, uncommitted changes so your working directory is clean enough to switch branches (for example to handle an urgent hotfix), and git stash pop restores them later - it does not touch your commit history.

promptText: What is the purpose of Git's staging area (the index)?
options: It acts as a draft of your next commit, letting you deliberately curate exactly which changes get committed via git add
It is a temporary network buffer used only while pushing to a remote
It stores a compressed backup of every previous commit for fast lookup
It is a synonym for the working directory with no distinct purpose
explanation: The staging area sits between the working directory and the repository - git add moves a snapshot of a change into it, letting you craft a clean, deliberate commit from a messy working directory (git add -p even lets you stage only selected hunks of a file).

promptText: Why is it considered a serious mistake to rebase a branch that other developers have already pulled and built work on top of?
options: Rebase rewrites commits with new hashes, so teammates' history diverges from the rewritten branch and they hit confusing conflicts on their next pull
Rebase permanently deletes the original commits from the remote server for everyone simultaneously
Rebasing shared branches is technically blocked by Git and will always fail with an error
Rebase only works on branches with fewer than 10 commits, so it fails silently on larger shared branches
explanation: Rebase replays commits as brand-new objects with new hashes; if teammates already have the old commits, their local history now shares no common lineage with the rewritten branch, causing confusing divergence and duplicate-looking conflicts - the rule is to rebase only private, unpushed work and merge to integrate shared branches.

promptText: What distinguishes a fast-forward merge from a three-way merge?
options: A fast-forward simply moves the branch pointer forward because there was no divergence; a three-way merge uses the common ancestor plus both tips to compute a result and creates a merge commit
A fast-forward always creates a merge commit, while a three-way merge never does
A three-way merge is only used when merging exactly three branches at once
A fast-forward merge requires manual conflict resolution, while three-way merges never conflict
explanation: When the target branch hasn't diverged, Git can just move the pointer forward with no new commit (fast-forward); when both branches have new commits since diverging, Git computes the result using the two tips plus their merge base and records a merge commit with two parents (a three-way merge).

promptText: Git never stores an explicit 'rename' operation for a file. How does it still detect that a file was renamed?
options: Tools like diff and log compare a deleted path in one tree against an added path in another and flag it as a rename if the blob content is similar enough (by default at least 50%)
Git stores a hidden metadata field on every blob recording its original filename
Renames are detected by matching file creation timestamps between the two trees
Git cannot detect renames at all; every rename always appears as an unrelated delete and add
explanation: A tree is just a name-to-blob mapping, with no 'rename' object type - rename detection is a similarity heuristic applied after the fact by tools like git diff -M, comparing deleted and added paths' blob content; heavily editing a file in the same commit as renaming it can push similarity below the threshold and it will show as a plain delete+add instead.

promptText: Why does git gc pack loose objects into packfiles rather than leaving every object as its own file?
options: Packing applies delta compression between similar objects (e.g. successive versions of the same file), making storage and network transfer dramatically smaller than many individually compressed loose objects
Packing is purely cosmetic and has no effect on repository size or performance
Loose objects are actually faster to transfer over the network than packed ones
git gc packs objects only to satisfy filesystem limits on the number of files in a directory
explanation: Loose objects are each individually zlib-compressed with no relationship to other objects; git gc collects them into a packfile using delta compression against similar base objects, which is far more space-efficient - this is also the same packfile mechanism used to transfer data during push/fetch.

promptText: How does git bisect locate the exact commit that introduced a regression so efficiently?
options: It performs a binary search between a known-good and known-bad commit, checking out the midpoint each time, finding the culprit in roughly log2(n) steps
It runs every test on every commit in the range sequentially from oldest to newest
It uses machine learning to predict which commit is most likely to be the cause
It only checks the most recent 10 commits regardless of how large the range is
explanation: git bisect halves the remaining commit range on each good/bad report, converging on the first bad commit in roughly log2(n) steps instead of a linear crawl - git bisect run automates the whole loop with a pass/fail script, exit code 0 meaning good and non-zero meaning bad.

promptText: Why can't a client-side pre-commit hook be relied upon as an actual compliance control?
options: Hooks live only in the local, unversioned .git/hooks/ directory and are not transferred by clone or push, and can be bypassed with --no-verify
Client-side hooks require a paid GitHub/GitLab subscription to function at all
Pre-commit hooks can only check spelling errors, not security-sensitive content like secrets
Client-side hooks automatically disable themselves after 30 days for security reasons
explanation: Since .git/hooks/ is not versioned content, hooks are never distributed to a new clone and require separate setup tooling to install, and even when installed, a developer can skip them entirely with --no-verify - real enforcement requires a server-side hook (pre-receive) or, more commonly, a required CI check enforced via branch protection.

promptText: A developer accidentally deletes a branch with an unpushed commit. Weeks later they try to recover it via reflog and find nothing. What most likely explains this, given Git's default reflog expiration settings?
options: The reflog entry for that now-unreachable commit likely expired after 30 days (gc.reflogExpireUnreachable), and a subsequent git gc pruned the object since nothing referenced it anymore
Reflog entries for deleted branches are removed immediately, within seconds of the branch deletion
Reflog only tracks tag operations, never branch deletions, so this was never recoverable in the first place
The commit is still fully recoverable indefinitely; reflog entries never expire under any configuration
explanation: Reflog entries expire by default after 90 days if still reachable via some ref, but only 30 days if already unreachable (as a deleted branch's commit would be); once that entry expires, a later git gc is free to actually prune the now-truly-unreferenced object, at which point it is genuinely gone and git fsck will find nothing - Git's safety net is a generous default window, not an absolute guarantee.

promptText: A large engineering org wants engineers to have full commit-history navigation (log, blame, bisect across all of history) but doesn't want every clone to download every historical file version upfront. Which cloning strategy fits, and why doesn't a shallow clone work instead?
options: A partial clone (--filter=blob:none) fetches the full commit graph but lazily fetches file content on demand; a shallow clone truncates history depth itself, breaking log/blame/bisect beyond the shallow boundary
A shallow clone is the correct choice here since it also preserves the full commit graph while only fetching recent blobs
Sparse-checkout alone solves this because it prevents blob objects from ever being fetched from the remote
Neither shallow nor partial clone can achieve this; only Git LFS can separate history from blob content
explanation: A shallow clone truncates the number of commits fetched, which cripples log, blame, and bisect beyond that boundary; a partial clone instead keeps the full commit graph intact (so history navigation works normally across all of history) while omitting blob content, fetching it lazily from the promisor remote only as files are actually checked out or diffed - sparse-checkout only affects what's materialized in the working directory, not what's fetched.

promptText: Two PRs each pass their required CI status checks independently against the current main and are both approved. After merging both back-to-back, main breaks. What gap does a merge queue close that required status checks alone do not?
options: Required status checks only verify each PR was tested against main separately, not that the combined result of both merging together also passes; a merge queue serializes merges and re-tests each PR against the very latest main immediately before merging
Required status checks are purely cosmetic and never actually run any CI job before merge
A merge queue works by preventing more than one PR from being opened at the same time across the whole repository
This scenario is impossible if required status checks are enabled, since they guarantee any two approved PRs are always compatible
explanation: Passing CI on each PR individually only proves each one is compatible with main as it existed at that PR's test run - it says nothing about whether the two changes are compatible with each other once both have landed. A merge queue closes this gap by serializing merges and re-testing each PR against the latest main right before merging, guaranteeing changes are 'tested together, not just tested separately.'
